trips.title: Who makes the decisions?
trips.goal: We are learning how people can have a say in local decisions.
trips.invitation: Step inside the place where Surrey makes decisions.
trips.route: Watch selected parts of the tour together. Pause when a room or service gives you a clue about who does what. Keep one question for your civic case wall.

stops.title: A place to decide
stops.notice: Look for the council meeting space or a description of council’s work.
stops.question: What decision might be made here?

stops.title: People doing the work
stops.notice: Notice a city service or department mentioned in the tour.
stops.question: Who turns a council decision into something people can use?

stops.title: A voice that is missing
stops.notice: Think of someone affected by your class’s chosen issue.
stops.question: What would you need to ask them before deciding?

trips.task: For the fictional recreation-centre choice, identify who decides, who carries out the decision and whose view you still need.
trips.entry: Name a person who uses a shared recreation space. What might they need?
trips.extension: Compare the City’s explanation with a community source. What does each help you understand?
trips.check: Can you explain the difference between making a decision and carrying it out?

fallback.title: Who makes the decisions? · text and table-top route
facts: Surrey’s council makes local decisions; city staff carry out the work of city departments.
People affected by a decision may have different needs and different opportunities to be heard.
A City-produced tour explains the institution’s work. It cannot speak for every resident.
fallback.action: Imagine the class is choosing where to put a new reading corner. Name who decides, who sets it up, and whose needs must be heard. Transfer those three roles to your civic issue.

teacher.placement: Voice and Rules, decision-making screen (step 6). Use selected council/services excerpts within the source-review time. The class recreation-centre scenario remains fictional.
teacher.prepare: Preview a short council/services excerpt. The full video is about 17 minutes; do not add the whole video to this lesson. Board or paper is enough.
teacher.model: Council could decide to fund a park upgrade. Staff would organize the work. We still need to hear from people who use the park.
teacher.misconception: The mayor does not make every decision alone. A promotional tour is one institutional perspective, not proof that everyone has equal influence.
teacher.assessment: Check for distinct decision-making and implementation roles and a relevant missing perspective. Return to the lesson’s existing decision task.
teacher.curriculum: Social Studies 6: government systems and civic participation; local context supports comparison with other systems.
teacher.sourceNotes: Official City tour page links this video and the student workbook. The fictional class-space activity is our teaching analogy.
teacher.verification: Daryl confirmed direct video access. On 2026-09-05 the browser loaded a 17:02 player, but media time did not advance, so this is not an observed playback pass. No captions were available in that player state. Embedded and school-network playback remain untested.
grades: K–2: use one brief excerpt and discuss a fair choice for a shared space.
Grades 3–5: name who decides and one person to ask.
Grades 6–8: connect authority, evidence and participation.
Grades 9–12: compare formal participation with practical access and accountability.
teacher.logistics: Recorded or self-guided public resource; no live booking or event time. No price or account request was encountered on the reviewed source route. School-network access is untested. English text backup is included; caption availability must be checked on the chosen player.

trips.title: Swim along with a sea turtle
trips.goal: We are learning to separate what we observe from what we assume about an animal.
trips.invitation: What changes when the camera travels with a turtle?
trips.route: Watch a short section. Pause on one clear frame, then another after the camera has moved. Gather exact words before imagining a story.

stops.title: Describe one frame
stops.notice: Name a visible colour, shape, texture or movement.
stops.question: Which word is most precise?

stops.title: Change the viewpoint
stops.notice: Compare what becomes visible after the camera moves.
stops.question: What can you see now that you could not see before?

stops.title: Separate seeing from guessing
stops.notice: Choose one observation and one imagined idea.
stops.question: Which could a classmate check in the footage?

trips.task: Share one visible movement or habitat detail and one question that needs another source. Return to the animal-care evidence before recommending an action.
trips.entry: Say two observations to a partner, or sketch one frame and label it.
trips.extension: Rewrite one line from a different camera position. Explain what changed.
trips.check: Did you separate a camera observation from a claim about the animal’s needs or feelings?

fallback.title: Swim along with a sea turtle · text and table-top route
facts: This WWF footage comes from a camera carried by a turtle. It follows the camera’s position.
The camera does not show exactly what the turtle’s eyes see or what it thinks.
A poem can include imagination, but we should not present an invented animal thought as a scientific finding.
fallback.action: Place a pencil case on a desk. Observe it from above and from seated desk height. Collect five precise words. Write two lines; label any imagined voice as fiction.

teacher.placement: Animal Welfare, opening observation. Replace the generic noticing example with a brief turtle-camera excerpt, then return to the existing care evidence and action. The video cannot establish a welfare verdict.
teacher.prepare: Preview two clear frames. Plan 2–3 minutes of footage and 4–5 minutes for words and talk. An actual desk object supports the backup.
teacher.model: “The view tilts and the reef passes below” is an observation if visible. “I am searching for a friend” is an invented turtle voice.
teacher.misconception: An animal-mounted camera is not a model of animal vision or a source of animal-care advice.
teacher.assessment: Listen for an observed detail, a clearly labelled uncertainty and a question for another source. Keep the existing care-recommendation task.
teacher.curriculum: English Language Arts 6: sensory detail, creative language and distinguishing evidence from inference. Animal ecology is enrichment.
teacher.sourceNotes: The WWF-Australia video is corroborated by its official channel playlist. No exact timestamps or biological sensory claims are assumed.
teacher.verification: Source reviewed 2026-09-05. Player or source metadata checked; sustained video playback, lesson embed and school-projector use still need confirmation. Use the prepared text route if video cannot play.
grades: K–2: notice two visible things without guessing feelings.
Grades 6–8: explain the limit of camera evidence.
Grades 9–12: discuss how recording tools shape evidence.
